text: In this early laparoscopic sequence spanning frames 832 through 896, we have an initial panoramic view of the upper abdomen during the exploratory and setup phase of the procedure. No surgical instruments are actively deployed in the frame during this interval, as the laparoscope gently adjusts its position to survey the regional anatomy. Readily identifiable structures include the inferior edge of the liver, the prominent vertical band of the falciform ligament with the ligamentum teres hepatis on the right, and the anterior wall of the stomach and greater omentum inferiorly. Across frames 848 to 880, the camera maintains a stable diagnostic angle assessing intra-abdominal morphology and space creation prior to initiating traction on the gallbladder fundus. At this stage, the dissection for the Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet commenced (0/3 criteria met), as exposure of the hepatocystic triangle is pending. Operative difficulty appears low to standard at this juncture, characterized by generous working space under pneumoperitoneum despite moderate adiposity, and without gross evidence of acute peritonitis or dense subhepatic adhesions. By frame 896, the view stabilizes in preparation for introducing working graspers to elevate the liver and expose the gallbladder.

In this sequence spanning frame 912 to frame 976, we observe the initial exploratory phase of the laparoscopy prior to beginning the cholecystectomy dissection. The laparoscope provides an overview of the upper abdomen, where the anterior abdominal wall, the falciform ligament with its prominent vascularization, the inferior edge of the liver, and the underlying greater omentum and stomach are clearly visualized. Across frames 928 and 944, the camera maintains orientation within the peritoneal cavity without active surgical instruments yet engaged in tissue manipulation. Diagnostic laparoscopy confirms normal liver parenchyma and unremarkable surrounding viscera, with no obvious signs of cirrhosis, acute gross peritonitis, or dense adhesions visible in this quadrant. By frame 976, exposure is being planned to elevate the liver edge and access the gallbladder and hepatocystic triangle. At this opening stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet been addressed, and the baseline procedural difficulty remains standard.

In this initial sequence spanning frames 992 to 1056, we observe the exposure phase of the procedure. Cephalad traction is being maintained on the gallbladder fundus, elevating the liver and bringing the subhepatic anatomy into view. Clearly visualized in the operative field are the inferior border of the liver, the gastric antrum/duodenum inferiorly, and adjacent omental attachments. The camera provides a stable diagnostic inspection to assess the degree of inflammation and anatomical orientation before beginning dissection. The Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet been addressed, as dissection within the hepatocystic triangle is yet to commence. The operative field appears clean with low baseline inflammation, suggesting favorable tissue planes and low technical difficulty at this opening stage.

In this sequence from frame 15750 to 15766, we are in the gallbladder dissection phase, separating the gallbladder body from the hepatic bed. A monopolar hook electrocautery enters from the right, while a laparoscopic grasper from the left provides steady lateral and anterior counter-traction on the infundibulum and neck. Retraction of the fundus is maintained superiorly, presenting excellent exposure of the peritoneal reflection and cystic plate. Multiple surgical clips are clearly visible along the previously divided cystic pedicle, confirming that the critical view of safety (CVS) was already achieved and the cystic duct and artery have been safely transected. Progressing through frames 15782 to 15814, the hook applies gentle hook-and-pull electrocoagulation to divide the loose areolar attachments in the liver bed. The operative field remains clean and bloodless with minimal baseline inflammation, representing low procedural difficulty. The surgeon properly stays within the avascular subserosal plane, carefully avoiding both liver parenchymal injury and perforation of the gallbladder wall.

In this short sequence spanning frames 15830 to 15894, we observe the active dissection phase aiming toward establishing the Critical View of Safety (CVS). A Maryland or toothed grasper retracts the gallbladder body and infundibulum superiorly and laterally, providing critical counter-traction on the peritoneal reflection. An L-hook electrocautery enters from the right-hand port to carefully score and divide the thin fibroperitoneal attachments along the infundibulum and cystic plate junction (notably seen engaging tissue from frame 15830 through 15878, with tissue division evident by frame 15894). The underlying liver parenchyma of segment V, the gallbladder wall, and the inferior omental structures are clearly visible with minimal inflammation or scarring. At this stage, CVS is partially developed: the hepatocystic triangle is undergoing clearance of fat and fibrous tissue, and initial mobilization of the lower gallbladder from the cystic plate is underway. Overall, anatomical planes are well-defined, hemostasis is pristine, and the case presents a low degree of operative difficulty.

Across frames 19500 through 19564, we are in the gallbladder detachment phase, separating the gallbladder from the hepatic bed. An electrosurgical hook is positioned at the junction between the gallbladder and the liver fossa, utilizing monopolar cautery to divide the remaining areolar and peritoneal attachments. Traction and countertraction are maintained by graspers out of view and along the peripheral field, keeping the subserosal plane under optimal tension. The exposed liver bed is dry with minimal charring, and the dissection plane remains clean and well-developed. Because the cystic duct and artery have already been clipped and divided, the Critical View of Safety has previously been accomplished. Advancing slowly through frames 19532 to 19564, the hook applies short pulses of energy while staying parallel to the liver capsule to avoid parenchymal injury or gallbladder perforation. Overall, the tissue handling reflects low procedural difficulty with favorable, non-inflamed anatomy.

During this sequence (frames 19580–19644), we are in the gallbladder detachment phase, separating the gallbladder body from the liver bed along the cystic plate. A monopolar hook electrocautery instrument is utilized to carefully divide the serosal and fibrous attachments at the peritoneal reflection. Across frames 19580 to 19612, the hook engages the tissue plane, and from frames 19628 to 19644, controlled energy is applied to dissect the connective tissue while maintaining the dissection strictly on the gallbladder wall to avoid liver parenchymal damage. Strong, steady traction and counter-traction are maintained by an assistant grasper visible on the right, keeping the dissection plane wide and clearly exposed. Relevant anatomical landmarks include the liver bed (gallbladder fossa), hepatic parenchyma, and the gallbladder wall being peeled away. The Critical View of Safety (CVS) was established and documented prior to this step, with the cystic duct and artery already secured. The surgical difficulty remains low to moderate given the clean tissue plane, good exposure, and absence of acute inflammation or active bleeding.

In this sequence spanning frames 19660 to 19724, we observe the gallbladder detachment phase from the liver bed. An electrocautery hook is utilized at the apex of dissection (frames 19660–19708) to carefully score and divide the peritoneal and fibroareolar attachments connecting the gallbladder to the cystic plate. The operative field displays the liver parenchyma, the bare hepatic bed, and the adjacent omentum inferiorly. By frame 19724, an auxiliary grasper is introduced from the left to re-grasp and elevate the gallbladder, applying effective countertraction to open the avascular dissection plane. The Critical View of Safety was successfully established in earlier steps prior to the division of the cystic duct and artery. Dissection proceeds smoothly with minimal oozing, low anatomical difficulty, and excellent preservation of the underlying liver capsule.

In this sequence between frames 19740 and 19804, we are in the gallbladder dissection phase, separating the gallbladder from the liver bed. In frame 19740, the cystic duct and artery have already been clipped and divided, with secure clips clearly visible at the base of the infundibulum confirming that the Critical View of Safety was established earlier. From frame 19756 to 19772, an atraumatic grasper from the working port is placed against the gallbladder body while the fundus remains retracted cephalad. The surgeon rotates and rolls the gallbladder medially and superiorly across frames 19772 to 19788, clearing the lateral peritoneal folds and developing optimal countertraction against the cystic plate. By frame 19804, the grasper shifts to reposition higher on the gallbladder neck/body junction, providing direct exposure of the remaining attachments on the posterior hepatic bed. The surgical field displays favorable anatomy with minimal inflammation (Parkland grade 1–2), allowing for clean, controlled mobilization with clear visualization and excellent hemostasis.

In this sequence spanning frames 19900 to 19964, the procedure has advanced into the gallbladder detachment phase, freeing the gallbladder body and fundus from the liver bed. At frame 19900, the Critical View of Safety has already been successfully accomplished earlier in the case, evidenced by the clipped and divided cystic structures visible along the lower margin. A left-hand grasper applies continuous countertraction to the gallbladder wall, maintaining adequate tension across the remaining attachments to the cystic plate. Across frames 19916 to 19948, the dissecting instrument meticulously develops the avascular retrocholecystic plane, ensuring dissection stays strictly on the gallbladder wall to avoid liver parenchymal injury. By frame 19964, an auxiliary instrument (suction cannula) enters from the superior port to assist with clearance and field optimization. Dissection conditions remain favorable with low-to-moderate operative difficulty, demonstrating clean tissue planes and no active bleeding or biliary leakage.

In this series of frames (19980 to 20044), we are observing the gallbladder dissection phase, separating the gallbladder body from the hepatic bed. Two grasping forceps maintain coordinated upward and lateral counter-traction, displaying excellent exposure of the peritoneal reflection and the underlying liver bed. Entering the field in frame 19980 and advancing by frame 19996, the monopolar hook electrocautery engages the tensioned peritoneal attachment. Across frames 20012 to 20044, the surgeon precisely hooks and divides these fibers along the avascular plane of the cystic plate. Note that the critical view of safety (CVS) was established and documented earlier in the procedure, as evidenced by the secure surgical hemoclips already seated on the divided cystic structures inferiorly. The gallbladder exhibits mild chronic thickening, but the dissection plane remains clear and hemostatic, presenting moderate surgical difficulty handled with disciplined technique.

In this sequence spanning frame 1563 to frame 1627, we observe the initial exposure and positioning phase of the procedure. Visible anatomical structures include a moderately distended, tense gallbladder, the inferior surface of the liver, and the prominent fatty falciform ligament/ligamentum teres running anteriorly. At frame 1563, a laparoscopic grasper is seen contacting the dome of the gallbladder fundus to assess graspability and establish cephalad retraction. As the sequence progresses through frame 1579 to frame 1627, the grasper disengages and withdraws deeper towards the subdiaphragmatic space to readjust its trajectory and achieve a more secure purchase. Calot’s triangle dissection has not yet commenced, and the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is entirely unachieved at this early stage. The primary technical difficulty noted here is the tensely distended, slightly thickened gallbladder wall, which carries a risk of slippage or perforation if gripped aggressively before decompression.

In this introductory exposure phase across frames 1643 to 1707, we observe initial setup and liver retraction to properly expose the gallbladder. Visible anatomy includes the distended gallbladder fundus, the inferior edge of the liver, the falciform ligament with its associated preperitoneal fat being elevated superiorly, and the greater omentum inferiorly. In frame 1643, a grasping or retraction technique elevates the round ligament and adjacent fat against the anterior abdominal wall to create a clear working window. By frame 1659 through frame 1691, a laparoscopic grasper is advanced deep into the subhepatic space, targeting the gallbladder fundus for superior-cephalad traction. By frame 1707, the instrument shaft positions itself behind the liver edge to securely grasp and elevate the fundus over the liver dome. Dissection has not commenced, and the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is at 0 of 3 criteria met. The operative field exhibits straightforward anatomy without dense adhesions around the fundus, suggesting standard baseline surgical difficulty.

In this opening sequence, we observe the initial exposure phase of the laparoscopic cholecystectomy. At frame 1803, a fenestrated atraumatic grasper is positioned over the fundus of the gallbladder. By frames 1819 and 1835, the jaws are closed to secure a firm, non-crushing hold on the apex of the fundus. In frames 1851 through 1867, the grasper initiates cephalad retraction towards the right shoulder/diaphragm to elevate the liver edge and expose the infundibulum and hepatocystic region. Anatomically, the gallbladder appears mildly distended with visible superficial vascularity and a thin, pliable wall, resting against the visceral surface of the liver without dense pericholecystic adhesions. At this early stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet been achieved (0/3 criteria met), as dissection of the hepatocystic triangle is yet to commence. Overall surgical difficulty appears low, with clear tissue planes and favourable ergonomics facilitating straightforward primary retraction.

During this initial sequence spanning frames 1963 to 2027, we observe the exploratory and orientation phase following initial peritoneal entry and pneumoperitoneum establishment. The laparoscope pans smoothly upward across the anterior parietal peritoneum, clearly displaying the arborizing subdermal and peritoneal vasculature overlying the abdominal wall musculature. Inferiorly, the greater omentum is visible resting over the viscera, with the dark edge of the liver coming into view along the lower right quadrant in frames 1963 to 1979 before the scope angles further cephalad through frames 2011 and 2027. No surgical instruments have yet been introduced or engaged in dissection, reflecting standard diagnostic laparoscopy prior to secondary trocar placement. Assessment of the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is not yet applicable, as Calot’s triangle has not been approached. The peritoneal cavity appears clean with normal anatomy and no immediate evidence of gross adhesions or entry-related trauma, presenting routine operative conditions.

At frame 0, we begin with an initial diagnostic laparoscopy and abdominal exploration, surveying the upper quadrant before port setup and retraction. Visible anatomy includes the smooth, normal-appearing liver edge, the vascularized gastric wall, and the greater omentum. Around frame 16, the laparoscope momentarily advances close to the peritoneal surface, resulting in temporary underexposure and optical shadowing. By frame 32, the camera withdraws to establish orientation, displaying the hepatic surface along with adjacent peritoneal folds. Moving through frames 48 to 64, the field stabilizes, clearly demonstrating the relationship between the inferior margin of the liver, the gastric antrum, and dense omental adipose tissue. No working instruments have engaged tissue yet, and the Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not been initiated as Calot's triangle dissection is still well ahead. At this preparatory stage, procedural difficulty remains baseline with non-inflamed anatomical landmarks.

Across frames 80 through 144, we are observing the initial exploratory phase of the laparoscopic cholecystectomy prior to instrument introduction. The laparoscope navigates toward the right upper quadrant to assess the baseline peritoneal and subhepatic anatomy. Clearly visible are the inferior surface of the liver, the anterior abdominal wall, and a substantial drape of yellow greater omentum. Notably, in frames 96 to 144, the camera zooms closer to inspect adhesions between the omentum and the inferior edge of the liver, which currently conceal the gallbladder and Calot’s triangle. No working instruments are present in the field of view yet, as the primary objective here is visual orientation and surveying for secondary pathology or prior adhesions. At this early juncture, the Critical View of Safety cannot be evaluated because dissection has not commenced. Surgical difficulty is moderately increased by the omental adhesions and prominent adiposity, indicating that gentle adhesiolysis will be required first to mobilize the omentum and expose the gallbladder fundus and infundibulum.

Across frames 160 to 224, we begin the procedure with an initial diagnostic laparoscopy and right upper quadrant inspection. The laparoscope visualizes the anterior abdominal wall superiorly, the hepatic parenchyma on the right, and abundant greater omental fat draped over the subhepatic space. At this stage, no surgical instruments have entered the field, and the gallbladder remains concealed beneath the omentum and liver margin. Frame 192 captures momentary light flare and shadow as the optic is adjusted to assess regional anatomy and peritoneal surfaces. This corresponds to the initial exposure and exploration phase prior to trocar placement or grasper introduction. Critical View of Safety (CVS) criteria are currently 0 out of 3, as Calot's triangle is entirely unexposed. The presence of significant visceral adiposity will require deliberate atraumatic retraction of the omentum to establish safe operative exposure.

In these opening sequences (frames 240–304), we observe the preliminary exposure phase of the laparoscopic cholecystectomy following port placement and initial peritoneal insufflation. The operative field displays the anterior abdominal wall superiorly and to the left, the inferior edge of the liver to the right, and the redundant greater omentum overlying the viscera inferiorly. A fenestrated atraumatic laparoscopic grasper is advanced through the upper port across frames 240 to 272, angling down toward the subhepatic space. By frame 288 and frame 304, the surgeon brings the grasper into position to manipulate and sweep the omental fat away to identify the gallbladder fundus and liver edge. The gallbladder has not yet been elevated, and dissection within the hepatocystic triangle has not begun; thus, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is currently at 0 of 3 criteria met. The anatomical planes appear clear with unremarkable tissue quality at this initial survey, representing standard baseline operative difficulty.

In frame 320, we begin the initial exposure phase of this laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with a primary fenestrated grasper positioned in the upper quadrant while the gallbladder remains hidden beneath redundant greater omentum. An atraumatic grasper enters from the right in frame 336, engaging the bulky fatty tissue overlying the subhepatic space. Across frames 352 and 368, the surgeon applies blunt downward and lateral traction to peel the omental adhesions away from the gallbladder bed. By frame 384, this caudal retraction successfully uncovers the tense, pale fundus and body of the gallbladder beneath the inferior liver margin. At this preliminary stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet begun to be established. The operative difficulty is mild to moderate, mainly characterized by thick visceral adiposity that must be carefully cleared to safely visualize target anatomy.

In this early stage of the procedure, we are in the preparation and exposure phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. At frame 400, an open laparoscopic grasper is held in the upper-left quadrant while the gallbladder fundus and body are visualized nested beneath the inferior edge of the liver, with surrounding omental fat inferiorly. By frame 416 and 432, a secondary instrument briefly sweeps into view from the right to probe and clear the operative field before being withdrawn by frame 448. The primary grasper repositions and readies its jaws across frames 448 and 464, preparing to establish fundal cephalad retraction over the dome of the liver. The gallbladder wall appears relatively thin and distended without gross inflammatory induration or dense adhesions. None of the Critical View of Safety (CVS) criteria are met yet, as Calot's triangle dissection has not commenced. Overall, exposure is clean and operative difficulty is expected to be low based on these initial anatomical findings.

In these initial operative frames (480–544), we observe the exposure and retraction phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The field clearly displays the inferior edge of the liver, the underlying distended gallbladder fundus, and the adjacent transverse colon/greater omentum below. In frame 480, a secondary cannula or suction shaft momentarily stabilizes the anatomy on the right before retracting. Meanwhile, a fenestrated laparoscopic grasper is advanced from the upper-left quadrant across frames 496 and 512, aiming directly toward the gallbladder fundus. By frames 528 and 544, the grasper opens and positions its jaws over the fundus to apply cephalad traction over the liver edge. Anatomically, the gallbladder appears moderately distended but free of dense fibrinous or adhesions at this level, predicting standard initial operative difficulty. At this early stage, dissection within the hepatocystic triangle has not begun, and the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is entirely unachieved.

In this opening sequence spanning frames 561 to 625, we observe the initial exposure phase of the laparoscopic cholecystectomy, focusing on securing stable fundal retraction. At frame 561, a fenestrated laparoscopic grasper is advanced under direct vision toward the gallbladder fundus resting beneath the inferior border of the liver. Progressing through frame 577, the jaws open to align an atraumatic bite across the fundus. By frames 593 and 609, the surgeon securely grips the fundal wall, ensuring adequate tissue purchase without perforating or tearing the gallbladder. In frame 625, initial cephalad and lateral traction is exerted to elevate the liver edge and bring the body and infundibulum into better view. The visible anatomy includes the inferior surface of the liver, gallbladder fundus, and adjacent omental fat, presenting minimal adhesions and suggesting a low baseline operative difficulty. At this early stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is not applicable, as Calot's triangle has not yet been exposed or dissected.

In frame 641, we observe the initial exposure phase of the procedure, where an atraumatic laparoscopic grasper is introduced toward the gallbladder fundus. Across frames 657 to 673, the grasper engages the fundus to initiate cephalad retraction over the superior edge of the liver toward the right shoulder. By frames 689 and 705, traction is established, unfolding the infundibulum and beginning the process of exposing the hepatocystic triangle. Key anatomical structures visible include the hepatic parenchyma of segments IV and V, the anterior abdominal wall, the diaphragm, and the greater omentum inferiorly. The gallbladder itself appears moderately distended with prominent subserosal vasculature, but free of dense adhesions or gangrenous changes. At this preliminary stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) criteria are at 0 of 3, as no dissection has yet taken place. The case presents with low surgical difficulty thus far, making effective cephalad fundal retraction the immediate priority to prepare the field for lateral Hartmann’s pouch traction.

In this opening sequence from frame 801 to frame 865, we observe the initial exposure and preparation phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The primary operative anatomy is clearly displayed, showing a tense, pale gallbladder nestled beneath segment IV and the right lobe of the liver, bordered inferiorly by the omentum and superiorly by the diaphragm. At frame 801, a laparoscopic grasper is advanced through an accessory port toward the fundus of the gallbladder. Across frames 817 through 849, the surgeon carefully opens the jaws and positions them over the apex of the fundus, establishing an optimal purchase point without causing serosal injury. By frame 865, the grasper is closing onto the fundus to begin cephalad retraction, which is the essential first maneuver to expose the hepatoduodenal ligament and Calot's triangle. At this nascent stage, dissection has not commenced, and the Critical View of Safety (CVS) criteria are at 0 of 3. Anatomy is favorable with no dense fundal adhesions or severe acute inflammatory edema, indicating low technical difficulty for this initial step.

In this sequence from frames 508 to 572, we are in the initial phase of Calot’s triangle dissection. In frames 508 and 524, the assistant maintains steady inferolateral traction on Hartmann’s pouch using an atraumatic fenestrated grasper, which effectively places tension on the peritoneal reflection covering the hepatocystic space. The anatomy clearly displays a distended gallbladder, the right hepatic lobe, and the peritoneal fold spanning toward the infundibulum. By frames 540 and 556, the primary working instrument—a monopolar L-hook electrocautery—enters the operative field from the epigastric port and approaches the tissue planes. By frame 572, the hook tip is positioned directly over the peritoneal serosa of the gallbladder neck to initiate the anterior peritoneal scoring. At this introductory stage, the Critical View of Safety (CVS) is not yet achieved (0 of 3 criteria satisfied), as the hepatocystic triangle remains unopened and the cystic plate is not cleared. Overall operative difficulty is low, with delicate translucent serosa, pliable non-inflamed tissue, and clear anatomic visualization.

In these frames spanning index 588 to 652, we are in the initial exposure and adhesiolysis phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. An atraumatic grasper on the patient's left provides steady inferolateral traction on an omental adhesion tethered to the body and infundibulum of a markedly distended, hydrops-like gallbladder. From frame 588 through 604, the monopolar L-hook electrocautery engages the tensioned adhesion band close to its insertion on the gallbladder serosa. By frame 620 to 636, the hook elevates the band to create a safe dissection window away from the underlying bowel, which is gently swept inferomedially. At frame 652, electrocautery is applied to divide this fibrous tissue, clearing the anatomy to expose the hepatocystic triangle. The Critical View of Safety (CVS) is currently at a very preliminary stage, with none of its three criteria met yet. Surgical difficulty remains low to moderate at this juncture, though careful electrosurgical technique is mandatory to avoid thermal transmission to the adjacent duodenum and colon.

In these initial frames, we observe the adhesiolysis and gallbladder mobilization phase of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. At frame 668, an atraumatic grasper from the assistant port exerts inferior-lateral traction on an omental adhesion tethered to the body of the gallbladder, while the fundus is retracted cephalad by a superior grasper. The primary operator deploys an L-hook electrocautery instrument to mobilize and divide this peritoneal-omental band cleanly off the gallbladder surface, as seen in frames 684 and 700. The gallbladder appears moderately distended with translucent, thin walls and mild vascular congestion, but without signs of severe acute purulence or gangrene. By frames 716 and 732, the hook cautery continues gentle blunt and thermal division of the fibrous attachment to fully expose the infundibulum and cystic pedicle. The Critical View of Safety (CVS) has not yet been addressed at this early juncture, as clearing these adhesions is essential before entering the hepatobiliary triangle. Overall surgical difficulty remains low to moderate given the pliable tissue planes and absence of dense, scarred chronic inflammation.
